courseTitle: How IT Teams Work: Agile, Waterfall, Scrum, Kanban & Software Releases

slots.practicalActivity: Pick two real IT deliverables you can imagine actually being asked to do - one that suits Waterfall (e.g. migrating a database to a new server by a fixed cutover date, where the requirements are locked) and one that suits Agile (e.g. building a new internal reporting dashboard that business users will react to once they can click around in it) - and write out, phase-by-phase for the Waterfall one (Requirements, Design, Build, Test, Release, Maintenance) and sprint-by-sprint for the Agile one (Plan, Build, Review, Adapt, repeated), what actually happens at each stage. Then write 2-3 sentences explaining why swapping the two approaches would hurt each project.
slots.deliverable: A one-page written comparison: a 6-phase Waterfall breakdown for one real deliverable, a 2-3 sprint Agile breakdown for another, and a short written justification for why each approach fits its project.

slots.practicalActivity: Take this real business request: 'Our regional managers keep asking me for last month's numbers by email. I need a dashboard that shows revenue by region and by product category, updated automatically, so they can check it themselves.' Break it into 3 real user stories in the 'As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]' format - one for the revenue-by-region view, one for revenue-by-category, one for the automatic refresh - and write at least 2 concrete acceptance criteria for each (e.g. for the refresh story: 'the dashboard reflects the prior day's closed sales by 7 AM each morning, with no manual steps'). Then sketch a one-week sprint plan naming which story you'd tackle first and why.
slots.deliverable: 3 written user stories with at least 2 acceptance criteria each, plus a one-paragraph sprint plan that prioritizes them with a stated reason.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a Kanban board (on paper or a spreadsheet) with Backlog, To Do, In Progress, Review, and Done columns. Place the 3 user stories you wrote in the previous slot into Backlog, move your top-priority story into To Do, then simulate one full week by moving that story across every column to Done - writing one sentence at each transition explaining what specifically triggered the move (e.g. what a passed code review looks like before 'Review' becomes 'Done').
slots.deliverable: A populated Kanban board (photo or spreadsheet) showing at least one user story moved from Backlog through to Done, with a written note on what triggered each column transition.

slots.practicalActivity: Trace one of your user stories from the Scrum slot through the full Dev -> QA -> UAT -> Production chain: write what a developer would actually build in Dev, what a QA tester would check before promoting it (including at least one edge case, like a region with zero sales that month), what the business would need to confirm in UAT, and what 'released to Production' means for that specific story. Then write one sentence identifying which environment you'd investigate first if the dashboard breaks the day after release.
slots.deliverable: A written 4-stage trace (Dev, QA, UAT, Production) of one real user story including a QA edge case, plus a one-sentence answer on where to investigate a post-release bug first.

slots.practicalActivity: If you have Git installed, actually run: git init in a scratch folder, create a file, git add and git commit it with a specific descriptive message (not 'fixed stuff'), then git checkout -b to create a new branch and make a second commit on it. If you don't have Git installed, write out that exact command sequence in order with a one-line explanation of what each command does. Then diagram, in writing, how pushing that branch would move through a CI/CD pipeline - build, automated tests, staging deploy, production deploy - and write one sentence on what should happen automatically if the automated tests fail partway through.
slots.deliverable: Either a real local Git history (init, first commit, new branch, second commit) or a fully annotated command sequence, plus a written CI/CD pipeline trace for that branch that explicitly covers the automated-test-failure case.

slots.practicalActivity: Complete the Castlebridge Retail capstone end to end: finalize the 3 user stories and acceptance criteria you drafted earlier for the regional revenue dashboard request, move them across your Kanban board, write a short QA test plan that includes the zero-sales-region edge case, write a one-paragraph UAT sign-off in the sales director's voice (approving it or sending back specific feedback), write a specific release note (e.g. 'Added: Regional Revenue dashboard, refreshing daily at 7 AM. Known limitation: product category data is only available back to January' - not a vague 'various improvements'), and write up how you'd investigate a simulated production incident where a regional manager reports last month's numbers showing zero for their region two days after launch, plus what you'd communicate to them while still investigating.
slots.deliverable: A complete capstone packet: 3 user stories with acceptance criteria, a Kanban board showing story progress to Done, a QA test plan with the zero-sales edge case, a written UAT sign-off, a specific release note, and a production-incident investigation-and-communication writeup.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can explain how real IT teams plan, build, test, and release software -- Agile and Waterfall, Scrum and user stories, Kanban boards, the Dev/QA/UAT/Production chain, Git, and CI/CD -- and has practiced turning a vague business request into tracked user stories, a tested release, and a handled production incident, the same professional workflow a data science team ships models and dashboards through.
